He denies fevers, rash, weight loss, or recent infections.
There is no history of joint trauma or inflammatory arthritis.

No nodules or skin lesions are present.

lines: Worsening shortness of breath and fatigue with persistent cough and leg swelling.

encounters.cc: Follow-up visit 6 weeks after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement.

lines: Follow-up visit 6 weeks after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement.

This 67-year-old male with coronary artery disease, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and left ventricular aneurysm returns for follow-up six weeks after percutaneous coronary intervention with placement of a drug-eluting stent in the proximal left anterior descending artery for unstable angina, following his April 2020 evaluation for worsening heart failure symptoms.
He reports no chest pain or dyspnea and is adherent to his dual antiplatelet therapy.
His blood pressure and heart rate are well controlled.
Review of the stent placement report notes that the device was coated with paclitaxel.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
- Left ventricular aneurysm (status post myocardial infarction)
- History of duodenal ulcer disease (H. pylori eradicated)
- Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement (proximal LAD)
- Indomethacin 25 mg oral three times daily as needed for joint pain
Smoking: Former smoker, quit 10 years ago (20 pack-year history).

encounters.cc: Pleuritic chest pain and low-grade fevers for 2 weeks.

lines: Pleuritic chest pain and low-grade fevers for 2 weeks.

This 67-year-old male with coronary artery disease and left ventricular aneurysm presents to the emergency department ten weeks after percutaneous coronary intervention with a 2-week history of pleuritic chest pain and low-grade fevers.
He reports that the pain is sharp, worsens with deep breaths, and is relieved by leaning forward.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
- Left ventricular aneurysm (status post myocardial infarction)
- History of duodenal ulcer disease (H. pylori eradicated)
His medical history is significant for a myocardial infarction 6 weeks ago, for which he underwent percutaneous coronary intervention.
- Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement (proximal LAD)
- Indomethacin 25 mg oral three times daily as needed for joint pain
Smoking: Former smoker, quit 10 years ago (20 pack-year history).
His vital signs are stable, and there are no signs of hemodynamic instability.
On physical examination, a pericardial friction rub is auscultated.
Echocardiography reveals a small pericardial effusion without evidence of tamponade.
An ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevations and PR depressions.

encounters.cc: Neck pain and hand weakness after rear-end collision.

lines: Neck pain and hand weakness after rear-end collision.
The patient is a 68-year-old male with cervical spondylosis and coronary artery disease who presents to the emergency department after being involved in a rear-end collision while driving.
He denies loss of consciousness or lower extremity weakness.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
- Left ventricular aneurysm (status post myocardial infarction)
- History of duodenal ulcer disease (H. pylori eradicated)
His past medical history is significant for hypertension and cervical spondylosis.
- Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement (proximal LAD)
- Indomethacin 25 mg oral three times daily as needed for joint pain
Smoking: Former smoker, quit 10 years ago (20 pack-year history).
On physical examination, the patient has a reduced range of motion in his neck due to pain.
Neurological examination reveals decreased grip strength and impaired fine motor skills in both hands.
Sensation to light touch and pinprick is diminished in the upper extremities, more pronounced in the hands.
Reflexes are diminished in the biceps and brachioradialis but are normal in the lower extremities.
There is no bowel or bladder incontinence.
An MRI of the cervical spine shows no evidence of acute fracture but reveals chronic degenerative changes.

encounters.cc: Progressive shortness of breath over 2 weeks with orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

lines: Progressive shortness of breath over 2 weeks with orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
This 69-year-old male with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and left ventricular aneurysm status post myocardial infarction presents with progressive cardiopulmonary symptoms.
He states that over the past two weeks, he has had increasing difficulty climbing stairs or walking short distances without becoming breathless.
He also reports waking up in the middle of the night gasping for air and now needs to sleep propped up on three pillows.
He denies chest pain, fever, or recent illness.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
- Left ventricular aneurysm (status post myocardial infarction)
- History of duodenal ulcer disease (H. pylori eradicated)
His past medical history includes hypertension and a recent anterior wall myocardial infarction 3 months ago, which was treated medically.
- Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement (proximal LAD)
- Indomethacin 25 mg oral three times daily as needed for joint pain
Smoking: Former smoker, quit 10 years ago (20 pack-year history).
His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), blood pressure 102/66 mm Hg, heart rate 108/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air.
On exam, he appears mildly distressed and is using accessory muscles of respiration.
Lung auscultation reveals bilateral late inspiratory crackles at the bases, and there is no wheezing.
Cardiac examination reveals an S3 gallop.
There is mild bilateral lower extremity pitting edema.
Chest x-ray shows bilateral perihilar opacities consistent with pulmonary edema.
A Swan-Ganz catheterization reveals an elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.

encounters.cc: Progressive shortness of breath with reduced appetite and leg swelling.

lines: Progressive shortness of breath with reduced appetite and leg swelling.

This 70-year-old male with known heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and left ventricular aneurysm, previously hospitalized in July 2022 for similar symptoms, presents to the emergency department with progressive shortness of breath that has worsened over the past several days.
He reports waking up at night gasping for air and needing to sleep propped up on several pillows.
He denies chest pain, cough, or fever but mentions reduced appetite and mild leg swelling.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (diagnosed 2022-07-15)
- Left ventricular aneurysm (status post myocardial infarction)
- History of duodenal ulcer disease (H. pylori eradicated)
His medical history includes long-standing hypertension and a prior anterior wall myocardial infarction several years ago.
- Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement (proximal LAD)
- Indomethacin 25 mg oral three times daily as needed for joint pain
Smoking: Former smoker, quit 10 years ago (20 pack-year history).
On examination, he appears fatigued and dyspneic at rest.
Cardiac auscultation reveals a third heart sound, and pulmonary examination reveals bibasilar crackles without wheezing.
Jugular venous pressure is elevated while peripheral pulses are weak.
A chest radiograph shows increased vascular markings and small bilateral pleural effusions.
A pulmonary artery catheterization is performed for further hemodynamic monitoring.

encounters.cc: Progressive fatigue, lightheadedness, and melena over 2 weeks.

lines: Progressive fatigue, lightheadedness, and melena over 2 weeks.

The patient is a 70-year-old male with coronary artery disease, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and prior duodenal ulcer disease presenting with progressive fatigue, lightheadedness, and melena over two weeks.
He had acute pulmonary edema six months ago.
He reports getting winded while climbing stairs and feels dizzy when rising from a chair.
He has also noticed that his stools have turned dark and sticky, which he describes as "tarry." He denies vomiting, abdominal pain, or visible blood in the stool.
He has no fever, chills, weight loss, or recent changes in appetite, though he has felt mildly nauseated and has been eating less than usual.
He attributes his symptoms to "old age and arthritis slowing him down."
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (diagnosed 2022-07-15)
- Acute pulmonary edema due to left heart failure (increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure) (diagnosed 2023-01-15)
- Left ventricular aneurysm (status post myocardial infarction)
- History of duodenal ulcer disease (H. pylori eradicated)
His medical history includes hypertension, osteoarthritis, and a duodenal ulcer diagnosed several years ago during an evaluation for melena.
He was treated for Helicobacter pylori infection and completed a course of acid suppression therapy.
Since then, he has not had any recurrence of ulcer symptoms.
- Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement (proximal LAD)
His medications include lisinopril and indomethacin for chronic joint pain.
He manages his medications himself and does not routinely review them with his doctor.
Smoking: Former smoker, quit 10 years ago (20 pack-year history).
His blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg, pulse is 98/min, and respiratory rate is 16/min.
On examination, the patient appears tired and pale.
Abdominal examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding.
Rectal examination reveals black, tarry stool that is positive for occult blood.
He has no abdominal masses, hepatosplenomegaly, or signs of chronic liver disease.
